blocks.x: You can give your name. My name is Joy William.
Alright, when were you born? I was born in 1910. Could we get your exact birth date? October 25th. That's good. Were you born right here in New Orleans? I was born in New Orleans.
What part of town? I was born uptown, around Dries and Thurid.
You can just sit back and relax if you like. Sit back and relax. We can put this over a little bit nearer too. He won't bother us.
No, sit right there. Don't say nothing.
Maybe you'd like to watch the wheels go around.
Can I start off when I first started playing music?
Yes, what was the first instrument you started on?

My first instrument when I started playing was violin. I was taking violin lessons from a professor by the name of Professor Taylor. I was taking lessons from him for a while. I started taking lessons from Professor Poikins.
Was that Dave Poikins? Dave Poikins. I've heard it. A lot of them did.
I took a drum lesson from Dave Poikins for about two or three years. I was playing music. On music.
On music.
Then from then on we made up a little band of our own. And we played around town. I started out playing on tin pans. Pots and pans and different things.
Tell you about it. How old were you when you took up violin and you started on violin? I was 15. 15. You'd been playing on these tin pans and all I guess.

Well I was playing on tin pans too. So I liked the tin pans better than I did the violin. So I got me a set of drums. I started the Shining Shoes on Tronelet and St. Canal. And I bought my first set of drums from Groomwall Music Store. I had a dollar a week.
I was wondering a little bit more about your family. Did your father and mother play any instruments? Were they musicians or anyone else?

No they wasn't. They were more than the rest of me playing them tin pans than anything else. So they say someday I would be a musician. Well I bought the first set of drums. I brought them home and played on them. I didn't start to play in the band for about a month after that. That step was good enough. So I fooled around and played a good bit with a different, you know, parties, house parties. That time we had house parties, piano and drum. That was going big. So I got a couple of jobs playing piano and drum and I thought I was good enough to play in a band.
Who'd you play with on piano? I remember the piano.
Well the piano, I'd taken a few lessons on the piano but I wasn't too much.
Well you played piano yourself.
Well I didn't play too much.
Well I thought you meant you played house parties with a piano player.

I'd take lessons, no. You see, at that time when they had parties, people put on parties, well they'd have a drum and a piano, which would be a band. Well they didn't have nothing other than that. They always had a drum and a piano. And that went big. Sometimes they'd have four or five parties in the block. Well whoever would be playing, they'd say George William was playing so and so. Another piano player would be great, he'll be playing somewhere else. Big I Lloyd piano player. I used to play with him mostly all the time. And to start off, that's where I started off. So after a while I said, well I'm going to get in a big band someday. So I went by Mr. Poikins, Professor Poikins. He taught me, I go to his house, I take a lesson twice a week. Where did he live then? On 6th Street, King Brown and Drive.
Same place I guess I've heard of before. Several people told us they went there.
So I went through with him, so I went for myself. And some fellas came and hired me to play at the Hummin' Boyd Cabaret. With Kit Clayton's band.
Oh yeah, George Gaynor was about here. He used to go there, that's the first place he ever had.
That's where George Gaynor and Clayton was playing. I was playing with George Gaynor and Clayton at the Hummin' Boyd Cabaret.
Where was that exactly?
I was at Bienville and Murray.
Right.

Is the district still running then? The district was still running then. And we played there for years. I played there for about a year, maybe two years. As long as I was running, I went to the entertainers. You heard of the entertainers? Well I still played there a while. So from then on, Sam Morgan had a drummer by the name of Roy Evans. Well, Roy Evans got hit with a brick, appetite on a truck. And it seemed like the drummer that Morgan had, the drummer that was playing with Morgan got hit with a brick. Yeah. That told me, the drummer that played with Chris Kelly went with Morgan.
If you have to answer the phone, it's alright too. If we can stop it at any time or any time you want to stop. If you want to turn out. Tell her that you can answer. We can stop if you want to turn.
Keep on?
Yeah. I guess she started the phone.

So, Morgan, Sam Morgan's come by every night. He said, boy you're going to be a good drummer someday. He said, now you should show me how to put that left foot and right foot down and keep the time with the music. So after a while, Morgan needed a drummer. Well he'd take me to the boy, just like I tell you, the boy Roy was playing with Sam Morgan. That told me to go with Chris Kelly. You heard talk of him? Oh yeah. I worked with Chris Kelly for many years at the Bulls Club. That's where we started, the Bulls Club. Well I played with Chris Kelly for about three years. I had first just got married, just after I got married in 1925. And we played in different places, all out of town. And after I played with Chris Kelly, I quit Chris, went with Joyce McCoy, went with Joyce McCullen. I heard talk of him.
You had a brass band too, didn't you?

Well, McCullen did. But I never played in a brass band. I played with Joyce McCullen Orchestra. So, several nights, we had a rehearsal at my house on 4th Street. At the time, Bill Matthews and them Warren's drummer in the brass band, which is the Excelsior Band. You heard talk of the Excelsior Brass Band. Well, I was the youngest one in the band. I think I was 16 and a half years, 17 years old. The youngest man in the band.
Who else was in that? Who was the leader?
Peter Bocci.
Peter Bocci.

Peter Bocci was the leader of the band. So, the first one they take me out on the funeral was the bass drum by the name of Giles, that died, that played with the Excelsior Brass Band, I'd taken his place at the time.
Is that Albert Giles' father?
Yeah, that's Albert Giles' father. And the snare drum player was Cantrell. Oh yeah.
Old Man Cantrell.

That was the snare drum player of the band. Boy, you want me to call some of the men names in the band? Well, I think you can remember some of the others. Well, I think so. Joe Payan, baritone, no, mellophone. George the Hooker was the bass player. And they had Charlie Love on trumpet. I remember him. Pete. And George McCullen. Oliver Alcorn. Buddy Johnson on trombone. You know him?
I don't remember, I've heard of him.

Well, I had him. And that's when I started out in the brass band. Well, we played in the brass band. I played with the Excelsior Band for maybe two, three years. Then I left the Excelsior Brass Band, I went with the Tuxedo Brass Band, which the leader of the band was Eddie Jackson. Yeah, I put a talk of him.
Oh yeah, some big tuba players.
Yeah, well, I played with Eddie Jackson brass, and I played with the Tuxedo Brass Band for quite a while. Well, the band is, when Eddie Jackson died, the band is, went to pieces. So that told me.
When did he die about? I never, of course, got to know him or hear him. I wondered, do you remember about what year did you, 10 and a half?
I don't know if he died in, I think 30 or 35, I think around 35, 1935, I think. It had been a while.
How long were you in the Tuxedo Band?
I was in the Tuxedo Band for about two years.
At that time did they have the Young Tuxedo Band already or not? Like John Kazimierz Band, it hadn't been started.

They had the Tuxedo Brass Band. It was first run under Papa Celestan. And after Papa Celestan gave it up, Eddie Jackson, the bass tuba player, kept the band going. So, well, he changed different men at the time. Of course, I think I was a good bass drum player, so he stole me from the Excelsior Brass Band. So that's why I started off with them. Then I used to play with Eddie Jackson Brass Orchestra, too, you see. Eddie Jackson had an orchestra. And a dance band.
You told me he played string bass for a while, too. Well, I don't remember him playing string bass,
but I know he was one of the greatest tuba players we've ever had in the city of New Orleans.
He played tuba in the dance band then?
Dance band and walking. When you played a bass, you're a man walking. When you played a bass, you're a man walking.
We were talking about your drum set again. How big a cymbal do you use now? What kind
of cymbals do you have now? I use a 21 inch cymbals.
Are they Turkish?

Yeah, they're zinyin. The Turkish cymbals, that was run around 14, 22 or 21 inch too. Now that's what we use now. The regular good cymbals, most of the drummers, all the drummers don't use the same thing.
If you want to answer the phone number.
No, she can actually talk to me. Don't worry.

segments.title: Opening, birth in uptown New Orleans, setting up
segments.summary: Williams gives his name, says he was born October 25, 1910 uptown in New Orleans; interviewer settles him in with some chatter.

segments.title: First violin and drum lessons; tin pans and first drum set
segments.summary: He began on violin with Professor Taylor, took drum lessons from Dave Poikins, played on tin pans, and bought his first drum set on a dollar a week.

segments.title: Parents, house parties with piano and drum, lessons with Poikins
segments.summary: His parents were not musicians; he played house-party jobs with a piano player, then studied twice weekly with Professor Poikins.

segments.title: Hummingbird Cabaret with Kid Clayton and George Gaynor
segments.summary: His first band job was at the Hummingbird Cabaret at Bienville and Marais in the District, with Clayton and George Gaynor; he stayed a year or two.

segments.title: Phone interruption
segments.summary: Pause while a phone rings and the interviewer offers to stop.

segments.title: Sam Morgan's advice, Chris Kelly, and Joyce McCullen's orchestra
segments.summary: Sam Morgan encouraged him and he took over from a drummer to play with Chris Kelly at the Bulls Club for about three years, then with McCullen's orchestra.

segments.title: Joining the Excelsior Brass Band and its members
segments.summary: As a youngster of 16-17 he replaced the late Giles on bass drum in the Excelsior Brass Band under Peter Bocage, and names its members.

segments.title: Tuxedo Brass Band under Eddie Jackson
segments.summary: He left Excelsior for the Tuxedo Brass Band led by Eddie Jackson after Papa Celestin, played in Jackson's orchestra too, and praises Jackson as a tuba player; Jackson died c. 1935.

segments.title: Cymbals he uses now
segments.summary: On a later tape, Williams says he uses 21-inch Turkish cymbals and that drummers differ in their choices.
